title: The Formula of Concord: the will passive in the kindling of new motions
source_text: XX. Huc redit quod habet liber Concordiae in Epitome articulorum de quibus controversiae ortae sunt inter Theologos Augustanae confessionis capite de libero arbitrio sub finem. Quod, inquit, Lutherus scripsit, hominis voluntatem in conversione pure passive se habere: id recte & dextre est accipiendum, videlicet, respectu divinae gratiae in accendendis novis motibus. Hoc est, de eo intelligi oportet, quando spiritus Dei per verbum auditum, aut per usum sacramentorum hominis voluntatem aggreditur, & conversionem ac regenerationem in homine operatur. Postquam enim Spiritus Sanctus hoc ipsum jam operatus est, atque effecit, hominisque voluntatem sola sua divina virtute & operatione immutavit atque renovavit: tunc revera hominis nova illa voluntas instrumentum est & organum Spiritus Sancti, ut ea non modo gratiam apprehendat, verum etiam in operibus sequentibus Spiritui Sancto cooperetur. Relinquuntur igitur ante conversionem hominis duae tantum efficientes causae ad conversionem efficaces, nimirum Spiritus Sanctus & verbum Dei, quod est instrumentum Spiritus Sancti, quo conversionem hominis efficit. Hoc verbum homo certe audire debet: sed tamen ut illud ipsum vera fide amplectatur, id nequaquam suis viribus propriis, sed sola gratia & operatione Spiritus Sancti obtinere potest.
pass_a_gloss: XX. To this comes what the book of Concord has in the Epitome of the articles about which controversies arose among the Theologians of the Augsburg confession in the chapter on free choice near the end. What, it says, Luther wrote, that the will of man in conversion is purely passive: that is rightly & properly to be understood, namely, in respect of divine grace in kindling new motions. That is, it ought to be understood of that, when the spirit of God through the word heard, or through the use of the sacraments, takes hold of the will of man, & works conversion and regeneration in man. For after the Holy Spirit has already worked & effected this very thing, and by his divine power & working alone has changed and renewed the will of man: then truly that new will of man is the instrument & organ of the Holy Spirit, that it may not only apprehend grace, but also cooperate with the Holy Spirit in the works following. There remain therefore before the conversion of man only two efficient causes efficacious for conversion, namely the Holy Spirit & the word of God, which is the instrument of the Holy Spirit, by which he effects the conversion of man. This word man ought certainly to hear: but yet that he may embrace it with true faith, this he can by no means obtain by his own proper strength, but by the grace & working of the Holy Spirit alone.
pass_b_english: Thesis XX. The Book of Concord comes to the same thing in the Epitome of the articles in controversy among the theologians of the Augsburg Confession, toward the end of the chapter on free choice. 'Luther's statement,' it says, 'that in conversion the human will is purely passive must be taken rightly and properly, that is, with respect to divine grace in kindling new impulses. It refers to the moment when the Spirit of God, through the word heard or through the use of the sacraments, lays hold of a person's will and works conversion and new birth in him.

Once the Holy Spirit has worked and accomplished this, and by his divine power and working alone has changed and renewed the person's will, then that new will really is the Holy Spirit's instrument and organ: it not only lays hold of grace but also works together with the Holy Spirit in the deeds that follow.

Before a person's conversion, then, only two efficient causes remain that are effective for conversion: the Holy Spirit, and God's word, the Holy Spirit's instrument by which he brings about conversion. A person must certainly hear this word, but he cannot by any strength of his own manage to embrace it with true faith; that comes only by the grace and working of the Holy Spirit.'
